items.content:
hooks are avoidable. kernel events not so much. but lots of programs do things like read files, so a single event is not an IoC. i’m not going to explain all the theory and tactics of evasion in this thread. whole books are written on it. but in general, you are never going to completely avoid leaving events and telemetry. you cant get the effects of calling an API without calling the API (in most cases), thats why the API exists. Yes we are limited to using the operating system like other desktop applications. The idea is to avoid signatured patterns, IOCs, and keep your “score” below a threshold where it gets bubbled up into an alert that gets investigated. The goal isnt to cause no kernel events. The goal is to blend in. The ultimate goal is to look like a normal process or application. 

The vm postex is likely to help with that. Its also likely to aid in resilience against defenders making easy signatures of your implants builtin postex commands. It is not silent. It is also just another option or tool in your toolbox. Its not perfect or necessarily better than other options in all scenarios. Its worth having as an option. In every scenario, details will vary and the best option is based on the environment you are operating in.

items.content:
RT @GenThreatLabs: The scam page can hide the price. The SMS can’t. Unless your phone does it for them, the code is offered for autofill before you ever open the message that says “every week”.

We call it #BillBait. Seen in 🇵🇱 Poland, 🇨🇭 Switzerland, 🇩🇰 Denmark and 🇨🇦 Canada. The mechanism is one line. Beyond the regulated customer text, the message carries the domain and code in a machine-readable pair: "@​example[.]com #2976" 

iOS and Chrome match it to the site you’re on and put the code right above the keyboard. No opening a message, no retyping. You tap the suggestion — and you’re subscribed. The SMS stating price, frequency and unsubscribe instructions never got read. For a login code that’s convenience. For operator billing that code IS the payment authorization. No card, no 3DS, no second confirmation. It starts a recurring charge on your phone bill.

iPhone showed 14.99 zł and dropped the “every week”. Chrome showed everything inside a prompt wearing Google’s authority and designed to be dismissed in half a second with an approval.

How people get the message in the first place? Ads with large font saying “Verify your phone to get full access”, 14.99 zł every week in tiny text under the banner. Not an accident.

Open the whole SMS. Check the frequency. If it’s not what you clicked for, don’t submit. And check your bill. An unfamiliar premium SMS or operator billing line means something got authorized. Call your operator, ask who’s collecting, cancel it, dispute the charge. Marking the sender as spam doesn’t stop the charges.

Full analysis: https://t.co/MPmk23JU8v
#SMS #MobilePayments #DCB

RT @nexta_tv: 👀 Secret surveillance software discovered in Moscow schools: interactive whiteboards can record students and teachers

A Moscow teacher discovered software installed on interactive classroom whiteboards that can secretly activate the microphone, record conversations during lessons, and send audio files to servers operated by the city's Department of Information Technology.

The software has reportedly been installed remotely since August 2026. Every ten minutes, it checks for commands from a server. After recording, it deletes the audio file from the device. Neither students nor teachers receive any notification.

Here's the interesting part: the software was originally called “Lesson Audio Recording Agent.” It was later renamed to the much more innocent-sounding “Lesson Support Agent.”

According to Mediazona, traces of the software were found in at least three schools. A source told the outlet that the recordings were intended to be analyzed using AI to monitor what was being taught in classrooms.

Moscow's Department of Information Technology did not respond to journalists' questions. The scale of the system's deployment and what happens to the recordings remain unknown.

In Russia, even a classroom whiteboard can now become an informant.
